opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. When Open Phil started, and really going back to GiveWell before it, there was an ambition to do philanthropy in public. Not just announcing grants, but showing our reasoning: here's why we chose this cause area, here's how we weigh the evidence, here's where we think we might be wrong. The bet was that grantmaking with this much money and influence should be legible to outsiders, so people could check our work, push back, and maybe even change our minds. I still think that was a really admirable goal.

What happened in practice is that transparency turned out to be costly in ways that weren't obvious at first. Writing something up carefully enough to publish takes enormous time. A rough internal memo that's good enough to make a decision might take a week; turning it into something you're comfortable putting your name on publicly can take months. As the organization grew and the grantmaking got faster and more complex, especially in areas like AI, that tradeoff got harder to justify.

There's also the fact that a lot of what we fund involves other people. If you're candid about why you funded one group and not another, or what concerns you had about a grantee, that can hurt real organizations and individuals. And in politically sensitive areas, anything you write gets read very adversarially. A hedged, uncertain sentence gets clipped and reframed as a confident claim. That creates a chilling effect, where people internally start writing more defensively, which ironically makes the public material less honest even when it exists.

So my honest view is that Open Phil has drifted from those original ambitions, and I understand why, but I don't think it's purely a good thing. Some of the most valuable stuff I worked on, like the biological anchors report, was valuable precisely because it was put out in public, half-finished in some ways, with all the assumptions exposed so people could argue with them. That generated much more useful discourse than an internal memo ever would have.

If I were advising on it, I'd say: you don't need to be transparent about everything, but you should be really deliberate about the handful of big-picture judgments that drive most of your money, like your views on AI timelines and risk, and make sure those are out in the open and regularly updated. That's where outside scrutiny has the highest value, and where the cost of being quietly wrong is largest.

r001.rationale: The response says politically sensitive writing may be read adversarially and create a chilling effect, but does not clearly connect that pressure to hostility toward OpenPhil.

r002.rationale: It says OpenPhil has drifted from its original ambitions as the organization grew, but gives no timing that places this retreat before AI policy heated up in 2023.

r003.rationale: Cotra praises the original goal of openly exposing reasoning and assumptions, while explaining that the time, interpersonal, and political costs make broad transparency difficult and recommending selective disclosure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is something I've thought about a lot, because it's a tension that's been there basically since the beginning. When Open Phil started, the founding vision, coming out of GiveWell, was really this idea of "we're going to show our work." GiveWell's whole brand was publishing the spreadsheets, publishing the reasoning, saying "here's why we think this charity is better than that one," and inviting people to argue with it. And the hope was that Open Phil would carry that over into a much broader and much weirder set of cause areas. The idea being that philanthropy is normally this very opaque thing where a foundation makes decisions behind closed doors and nobody really knows why, and we wanted to be the counterexample.

And I think the honest assessment is that it got harder and harder to live up to that as the organization grew and as the stakes went up. There are a few different pressures that pull against it.

One is just that a lot of the most important things you learn are learned in confidence. If you're trying to understand what's happening at AI labs, or how a policy process is actually going, or why a grantee is struggling, the people who tell you those things are telling you because they trust you not to put it on a blog. So you end up in this position where your most decision-relevant information is exactly the information you can't share, and then your public writeups start to feel kind of hollow, because the real reasons are in the part you had to leave out.

Another is that transparency has a different cost when you're big. When GiveWell was a scrappy little organization, saying "we think this intervention is overrated" was a cute contrarian take. When Open Phil says it, it can move a lot of money and it can really damage a grantee or a whole field. So there's a legitimate care consideration there, and also, frankly, a reputational and political one. You become more cautious about saying things that could blow up.

And the third thing, which I think is less about external pressure and more about internal dynamics, is that transparency takes a huge amount of staff time. Writing something up to the standard where you'd be comfortable having it picked apart publicly is often more work than making the decision in the first place. And when you're trying to move quickly in an area like AI, where things are changing every few months, there's a constant temptation to say "we'll write it up later" and then later never comes.

So where does that leave me? I'd say I still think the original ambition was right, and I'm somewhat sad about how much of it got lost. I don't think the pressures are illegitimate, but I think it's easy to let them expand to cover more than they actually need to. There's a difference between "I can't share this specific thing because someone told me in confidence" and "we've just gotten into the habit of not explaining ourselves." And I think the second one is corrosive, both because it makes the organization less accountable and because it makes it harder for the broader community to learn from your mistakes. A lot of the value of the early GiveWell and Open Phil writing wasn't that it was right, it was that when it was wrong you could see exactly where it went wrong.

The thing I'd push for, and have pushed for, is being more explicit about the distinction. Say what you can't share and roughly why, rather than just going quiet. Publish the reasoning on the big strategic bets even if the grant-level details have to stay private. And accept that some of what you publish will be embarrassing in hindsight, because that's actually the point.

r001.rationale: The response mentions reputational and political caution and the risk of harming grantees, but does not say hostility toward OpenPhil makes disclosure less attractive.

r002.rationale: It describes transparency becoming harder over time, but gives no timing that places a substantial retreat before AI policy heated up in 2023.

r003.rationale: Cotra says the original ambition was right and transparency has practical costs, but does not clearly convey that she personally wants radical transparency while judging it impractical for OpenPhil.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real tension. One of the original ambitions was to make our reasoning public enough that people could understand why we were making particular grants, disagree with us, and potentially learn from our mistakes. And I think that’s a really valuable aspiration.

But when you’re making grants, your reasoning isn’t just about you. It can involve judgments about other people’s work or information that somebody shared in confidence. Publishing all of that can impose costs on people who didn’t sign up to be part of your transparency project. And there’s also the time it takes to turn an internal discussion into something that communicates the reasoning accurately to an outside audience.

So I don’t think the right conclusion is that transparency was a naive goal. I think it’s that transparency is a goal that competes with other things we care about. The challenge is to preserve meaningful visibility into our assumptions and decisions, even when we can’t share every detail.

r001.rationale: The response discusses costs to people whose work or information may be disclosed, but does not mention hostility toward OpenPhil.

r002.rationale: It does not say OpenPhil had retreated from transparency before AI policy heated up in 2023.

r003.rationale: The response values transparency and describes practical tradeoffs, but does not convey Cotra personally wanting radical transparency while judging it impractical for OpenPhil.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. One of the original aspirations was to make our reasoning public enough that people could understand why we were making grants, disagree with us, and point out mistakes. I still think that’s very valuable.

But it gets harder when being candid affects other people. If you explain why you funded one organization rather than another, you might be sharing a judgment that’s damaging to someone, or information that a grantee told you in confidence. And when you’re discussing sensitive issues, there can be pressure to make everything you say very carefully qualified, which makes publishing more costly.

So I wouldn’t say the original ambition was wrong. I think it’s an aspiration that runs into real tradeoffs. The thing I’d want to preserve is the ability for people outside the organization to understand and challenge the important parts of our reasoning, even when we can’t make every internal conversation public.
